blocks.content: CITIZENSHIP

blocks.title: Key Takeaways
items: Part II of the Constitution (Articles 5 to 11) deals with Citizenship at the time of commencement of the Constitution on January 26, 1950.
Article 11 confers exclusive power on Parliament to regulate the right of citizenship by enacting legislation.
Citizenship can be acquired through five modes: Birth, Descent, Registration, Naturalisation, and Incorporation of Territory.
Citizenship can be lost through three modes: Renunciation, Termination, and Deprivation.
India provides for single citizenship, meaning citizens owe allegiance only to the Union of India and not to individual states.
INTRODUCTION

blocks.content: Citizenship refers to the legal relationship between an individual and the State. A citizen enjoys full civil and political rights and owes allegiance to the State.
In India, the concept of citizenship is provided under Part II of the Constitution
(Articles 5 to 11). These articles deal with citizenship at the time of commencement of the Constitution
and empower Parliament to make laws regarding citizenship.
Citizenship is very important because only citizens enjoy certain Fundamental Rights such as Articles 15, 16, 19 and 29.
MEANING AND IMPORTANCE OF CITIZENSHIP
A citizen is a legally recognized member of a State. Importance of Citizenship:

items:
• Determines who can enjoy political rights
  • Right to vote and contest elections
  • Eligibility for government services
  • Protection by the State
  • Sense of belonging to the nation
Determines who can enjoy political rights
Right to vote and contest elections
Eligibility for government services

blocks.content: ARTICLE 5 – CITIZENSHIP AT COMMENCEMENT
A person was considered a citizen of India on 26 January 1950 if:

items:
• He was domiciled in India, and
  • Born in India, or
  • Either of whose parents was born in India, or
  • Ordinarily resident in India for at least 5 years
He was domiciled in India, and
Born in India, or
Either of whose parents was born in India, or
Ordinarily resident in India for at least 5 years

blocks.content: This article defined citizenship at the time of independence.
ARTICLE 6 – MIGRANTS FROM PAKISTAN TO INDIA
Article 6 deals with persons who migrated from Pakistan to India. Such a person was considered a citizen if:

items:
• He migrated before 19 July 1948 and was ordinarily resident in India, or
  • Migrated after 19 July 1948 and was registered as a citizen This provision was made due to partition.
He migrated before 19 July 1948 and was ordinarily resident in India, or
Migrated after 19 July 1948 and was registered as a citizen This provision was made due to partition.

blocks.content: ARTICLE 7 – MIGRANTS TO PAKISTAN
Article 7 states that:

items:
• A person who migrated to Pakistan after 1 March 1947
  • Shall not be considered an Indian citizen Exception:

ARTICLE 8 – INDIANS RESIDING ABROAD
Article 8 provides citizenship to persons of Indian origin residing outside India. Conditions:

items:
• Either parent or grandparent was born in India
  • Person registered as citizen at Indian consulate
Either parent or grandparent was born in India
Person registered as citizen at Indian consulate

blocks.content: ARTICLE 9 – TERMINATION OF CITIZENSHIP
Article 11 empowers Parliament to make provision with respect to the acquisition and termination of citizenship and all other matters relating to citizenship.
Article 9 states that:

items:
• If a person voluntarily acquires citizenship of another country,
  • He ceases to be an Indian citizen.
If a person voluntarily acquires citizenship of another country,
He ceases to be an Indian citizen.

blocks.content: India does not allow dual citizenship.
ARTICLE 10 – CONTINUANCE OF CITIZENSHIP
Article 10 provides that:

items:
• Every person who is a citizen under Articles 5–8 shall continue to be a citizen
  • Subject to provisions made by Parliament
Every person who is a citizen under Articles 5–8 shall continue to be a citizen
Subject to provisions made by Parliament

blocks.content: ARTICLE 11 – POWER OF PARLIAMENT
Article 11 gives power to Parliament to:

items:
• Make laws regarding acquisition of citizenship
  • Termination of citizenship
  • Other matters related to citizenship

blocks.content: Using this power, Parliament enacted the Citizenship Act, 1955.
CITIZENSHIP ACT, 1955
The Citizenship Act, 1955 provides five ways of acquiring citizenship:

items: By Birth
By Descent
By Registration
By Naturalisation
By Incorporation of Territory

A foreigner can acquire citizenship by:

blocks.content: OVERSEAS CITIZENSHIP OF INDIA (OCI)
OCI is not full citizenship. OCI holders:

items:
• Cannot vote
  • Cannot hold constitutional posts
  • Enjoy long-term visa benefits

blocks.content: CITIZENSHIP (AMENDMENT) ACT, 2019

items: Fundamental Rights under Articles 15, 16, 19, 29, and 30 are available ONLY to Indian citizens and denied to aliens.
Articles 5 to 11 do not lay down permanent provisions for citizenship; they only determined who became a citizen at the commencement of the Constitution.
An Overseas Citizen of India (OCI) cardholder is not a dual citizen, as the Indian Constitution strictly prohibits dual citizenship under Article 9.

blocks.content: CONCLUSION
Citizenship forms the foundation of a democratic State.
The Indian Constitution and Citizenship Act provide a clear and detailed framework for acquisition and termination of citizenship.
Understanding citizenship is essential to understand rights, duties and identity of Indian people.
